title: The World Is Held Together by Duct Tape?  Intel's Failed Bitcoin Chip Bet
gist: A forum poster who built bitcoin mining chips argues Intel's Blockscale ASIC was an incoherent project: Intel spent over $100 million in 2022, skipped its own dynamic-logic strength, shipped at about 35 J/TH versus Bitmain's 20 J/TH, and killed the line within a year. The author considers and rejects a process-tuning rationale (as SMIC used the MinerVa miner for 7 nm) and concludes nobody was really in charge.

insights.claim: Intel spent more than $100 million on its bitcoin mining chip in 2022 and ended up with nothing to show for it, according to a forum poster who designs BTC chips.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: An example of Intel capital misallocation during its turnaround years.

insights.claim: Intel's Blockscale mining chip did not use dynamic logic, even though Intel's CPU-derived depth in dynamic logic far exceeded that of mining-chip startups, which had made competitors nervous when Intel entered.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Intel failed to apply its own core design advantage to a new market.
insights.quote: Then the product came out, and I was stunned: they didn't use dynamic logic.
insights.locator: When we built our BTC chips

insights.claim: Intel's Blockscale launched in April 2022 at a typical 35 J/TH and best case 26 J/TH, while Bitmain was already at 20 J/TH, meaning Intel's cost per hash was at least twice as high.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: In mining ASICs J/TH is the single competitive metric, and Intel was not close to Bitmain.
insights.quote: A mining chip is judged on a single number: how many joules it burns per TH of hash rate.
insights.locator: A mining chip is judged on

insights.claim: Mining chips suit tuning a new process node because they are highly repetitive, tolerate low yield by disabling failed cores, convert hash rate directly into yield feedback, and remain sellable even at low yield.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Explains why crypto ASICs often appear as early customers on new foundry nodes.
insights.quote: A mining chip is highly repetitive and can tolerate lower yield, because you can simply disable the cores that fail.

insights.claim: When SMIC developed its 7 nm process, the MinerVa mining chip, reportedly from the same people as Canaan, ran on it per a TechInsights teardown and helped the new process work out its yield.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Crypto-miner tape-outs can be a leading indicator of a new node's yield ramp.

insights.claim: Intel launched the second-generation Blockscale in April 2022, and in April 2023 an Intel spokesperson confirmed the product line had reached end-of-life, while Intel was planning $3 billion of cost cuts in 2023.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Cost-cutting pressure cut short exploratory side bets at Intel.

insights.claim: Neither a process-tuning rationale nor a profit rationale explains Intel's Blockscale: process tuning needs a continuous flow of orders rather than a two-version run, and a profit play would have used Intel's biggest strength, so the poster concludes it was a project nobody was really in charge of.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Signals weak project governance at Intel in that era, relevant to judging its execution on new ventures.
insights.quote: That leaves one: this was a project nobody was really in charge of.

insights.claim: Intel had both of a company's most valuable resources, process technology and people, yet took the most careless approach and built its shortest-lived product with Blockscale.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Having assets is not the same as deploying them well; execution risk remains the Intel question.
insights.locator: A plan that could use BTC
